title: Shared Stretch

source.name: Original exercise; classic technique (suffix automaton, longest common substring)

statement:
Two DNA samples are written as strings `s` and `t`. Find the length of the **longest contiguous stretch** (substring) that appears in both. If they share no letter, print `0`.

**Input.** Two lines: `s` and `t`, lowercase letters only.

**Output.** One integer.
constraints: 1 ≤ |s|, |t| ≤ 20000 in this browser version (the idea scales to 10^6)
Lowercase letters a to z only
hints: Dynamic programming over all pairs of positions is O(|s| * |t|), about 4 * 10^8 steps for the largest inputs: too slow. We want something near linear.

A suffix automaton of s is a small automaton that accepts exactly the substrings of s, with at most 2 * |s| states. Walk t through it: if you can follow the next letter, the matching stretch grows by one.

If the next letter has no transition from the current state, follow suffix links (shorter suffixes of the matched stretch) until a transition exists, and reset the current length to the longest length of that state. The answer is the largest length seen.
editorial: Build the **suffix automaton** of `s` online, one letter at a time. Each state represents a set of substrings that end at the same positions in `s` (all its strings are suffixes of the longest one, `len[v]`); `link[v]` points to the state of the longest suffix that belongs to a different set. Appending a letter creates a state `cur` with `len = len[last] + 1`, adds the transition on that letter from `last` and then from every state on the suffix-link chain that lacks it; at the first state `p` that already has the transition to some `q`, either `len[p] + 1 == len[q]` and `link[cur] = q`, or `q` must be **split**: a clone with `len[p] + 1` takes over `q`'s transitions and link, the transitions of the chain that pointed to `q` are redirected to the clone, and both `q` and `cur` link to the clone. The automaton has at most `2|s| - 1` states and `3|s| - 4` transitions and is built in amortised `O(|s|)` (times the alphabet size for a dense table). To find the longest common substring, run `t` through the automaton keeping the current state `v` and the current matched length `l`: if the next letter has a transition, follow it and increase `l`; otherwise move along suffix links (setting `l = len[v]` each time) until a transition exists or the root is reached; if the root also has none, `l` stays 0. The maximum `l` over the scan is the answer. Total `O(|s| + |t|)`. Use an array of transitions per state for a small alphabet; a map per state for a larger one.

starter.python:
import sys

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
s, t = data[0], data[1]

solutions.python:
import sys

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
s, t = data[0], data[1]
nxt, link, length = [{}], [-1], [0]       # the suffix automaton of s: transitions, suffix links and longest lengths
last = 0
for ch in s:
    cur = len(nxt)
    nxt.append({})
    link.append(0)
    length.append(length[last] + 1)
    p = last
    while p != -1 and ch not in nxt[p]:
        nxt[p][ch] = cur
        p = link[p]
    if p != -1:
        q = nxt[p][ch]
        if length[p] + 1 == length[q]:
            link[cur] = q
        else:                              # split q: a clone that only represents the shorter strings
            clone = len(nxt)
            nxt.append(dict(nxt[q]))
            link.append(link[q])
            length.append(length[p] + 1)
            while p != -1 and nxt[p].get(ch) == q:
                nxt[p][ch] = clone
                p = link[p]
            link[q] = link[cur] = clone
    last = cur
v = l = best = 0                           # walk t through the automaton, tracking the longest suffix of t[:i] that is a substring of s
for ch in t:
    while v and ch not in nxt[v]:
        v = link[v]
        l = length[v]
    if ch in nxt[v]:
        v = nxt[v][ch]
        l += 1
    best = max(best, l)
print(best)
